query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the substitutional element X governs whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms during exposure above 900 °C by affecting the lattice mismatch and interfacial coherency between the evolving oxide and the alloy. In particular, alloys with Al are expected to form epitaxial, adherent protective oxides (such as Al2O3, potentially in combination with Cr2O3), while those with Mn or Si develop oxides with higher lattice mismatch, leading to cracked or spalled scales.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state prepared under identical processing conditions.
generation.intervention: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C.
generation.conditions: All alloys are tested under identical high-temperature (>900 °C) oxidative/corrosive environments with controlled initial microstructures.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice mismatch and interfacial coherency between the forming oxide layer (e.g., Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3) and the underlying alloy.
generation.mechanism: The element X alters the oxidation kinetics by influencing the growth and structure of the oxide scale. With Al, reduced lattice mismatch promotes the epitaxial growth of a continuous, adherent protective oxide, whereas Mn or Si lead to oxides that are less coherent and more prone to cracking or spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEAs with Al will develop continuous, coherent, and adherent protective oxide layers, while HEAs with Mn or Si will exhibit discontinuous, poorly adhered oxide scales with evidence of cracking or spallation under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: The baseline comparison is against HEAs with Mn or Si under identical exposure, which are predicted to form less stable oxides.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX HEAs in their single- or multiphase solid-solution state when exposed above 900 °C in controlled oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative differences in lattice mismatch and the extent to which synergistic effects (e.g., with Cr2O3) influence oxide stability remain to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrFeCoNiX HEA samples with X varied (Al, Mn, Si) under identical processing conditions. Expose all samples to a controlled oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for a fixed duration. Subsequently, perform detailed morphological and structural characterization of the oxide scales.
measurements: Characterization of the oxide layer morphology and coherence using SEM and TEM.
Quantitative assessment of lattice mismatch through diffraction techniques.
Phase analysis via XRD to verify the presence and quality of oxides such as Al2O3 and Cr2O3.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if, under identical conditions, HEAs with Al do not consistently exhibit significantly lower lattice mismatch and a more coherent, protective oxide layer compared to HEAs with Mn or Si.

drafts.hypothesis: The formation and persistence of a stable, coherent protective oxide layer in CrFeCoNiX HEAs is governed by how the substitutional element X affects the lattice mismatch and interfacial energy between the evolving oxide and the underlying alloy. In particular, when X = Al, the alloy tends to form a coherent, epitaxial Al2O3 (possibly synergizing with Cr2O3) scale at temperatures above 900 °C, whereas with X = Mn or Si the higher lattice mismatch leads to the formation of unstable, cracked, or spalled oxides.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in a single or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, with X being Al, Mn, or Si, manufactured under identical processing conditions.
drafts.intervention: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures exceeding 900 °C.
drafts.conditions: Tests conducted at >900 °C under a controlled oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, ensuring the same starting microstructural state across all alloy variants.
drafts.structural_mediator: The lattice mismatch and interfacial coherency between the forming oxide (e.g., Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3) and the metallic substrate.
drafts.mechanism: Element X alters both the oxidation kinetics and the eventual microstructure of the oxide scale. In the case of Al, its strong affinity for oxygen and its ability to reduce lattice mismatch promotes the epitaxial growth of a coherent, adherent, and thermodynamically stable oxide layer. Conversely, Mn or Si lead to oxides with higher lattice mismatch and poor interfacial compatibility, resulting in unstable scales prone to cracking or spallation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: HEAs containing Al will form continuous, coherent, and adherent protective oxide layers, while those containing Mn or Si will exhibit discontinuous, poorly adhered, and cracked oxide scales under identical exposure conditions.
drafts.baseline: The baseline comparison is against HEAs with X = Mn or Si, which are predicted to form less stable oxide scales under the same environmental and processing conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX HEAs in single- or multiphase solid-solution states when exposed to oxidative or corrosive atmospheres at temperatures above 900 °C.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of CrFeCoNiX HEA samples where X is independently varied among Al, Mn, and Si, ensuring identical processing to yield similar single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states. Expose all samples to a controlled oxidative atmosphere at temperatures exceeding 900 °C for an identical duration. Perform post-exposure characterization using SEM, TEM, and XRD to assess the morphology, coherence, and phase composition of the oxide scales.
measurements: Quantitative determination of the lattice mismatch between the oxide layer and the underlying alloy using TEM diffraction.
Evaluation of oxide layer morphology and the presence of cracks or spallation using SEM imaging.
Phase analysis of both the oxide scale and the substrate using XRD to confirm the formation of Al2O3, Cr2O3, or mixed oxides.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if HEAs with X = Al do not consistently show a significantly lower lattice mismatch and a more coherent, adherent protective oxide layer compared to those with X = Mn or Si under identical exposure conditions.
